Assumes a 365-day year. This is an illustrative calculation, not a forecast of Welsh generation.

This distinction becomes especially important when comparing gas-fired power stations with wind and solar installations, or assessing reserve capacity.

7. Electricity is not the same as total energy consumption

This is a substantial qualification to claims of Welsh energy self-sufficiency.

The combined Welsh energy report identifies total energy use of approximately 83.2 TWh in its underlying consumption assessment, of which approximately 13 TWh was electricity.

Most remaining energy consumption is associated with heat, transport and industrial processes. regen.co.uk

Consequently, Wales generating more electricity than it consumes does not mean that Wales currently produces enough energy to satisfy all its energy requirements.

Future electrification of transport, industrial processes and heating may also materially increase electricity demand.

8. Renewable electricity targets

The Welsh Government’s stated targets are for renewable electricity generation to equal:

Target year	Share of annual electricity consumption
2024 — achieved	55%
2030 — target	70%
2035 — target	100%

0%55% achieved100%

The original March 2026 publication reported 54% for 2024. Following the August correction, the official figure increased to 55%. The revised figure should be used throughout the inventory. GOV.WALES +1

These are annual energy-equivalence targets, rather than commitments to supply every hour of Welsh electricity demand exclusively through renewable generation.

9. Implications for the sovereignty assessment

The current electricity system operates at an integrated British level, with international interconnections.

The economic and strategic assessment should therefore distinguish the following:

Value category	Relevant measurement
Productive activity	Actual electricity generation
Domestic requirements	Welsh electricity consumption
External supply	Net and gross cross-border flows
Dispatchable capability	Generation available when required
System flexibility	Pumped storage, batteries and balancing
Network infrastructure	Transmission, distribution and interconnection
Local economic return	GVA, employment, ownership income and taxation
Future resource potential	Further renewable and other generating capacity

A hypothetical independent Wales could continue to participate in an integrated electricity market, subject to negotiated regulatory, commercial and system-operation arrangements.

Independence would not inherently require electrical isolation.

Equally, the market value of all electricity generated within Wales should not be treated as Welsh Government revenue. Ownership, generation costs, imported fuel, commercial contracts and taxation determine how much economic value is retained.

“The extent to which Welsh electricity is exported or supports the wider grid

Welsh electricity infrastructure contributes to the wider British electricity system in two fundamentally different ways:

* Energy supply: electricity generated within Wales and transferred to other parts of Britain.
* System support: generating capacity, energy storage, frequency response, balancing and other services that help maintain the reliability of the wider electricity network.

The second category is particularly important. An annual net export figure can substantially underrepresent the contribution of infrastructure that provides electricity or stabilises the grid during periods of exceptional demand.

Wales’s pumped-storage facilities are an especially good example of this distinction.

1. Actual electricity exports: a declining historical surplus

There is an important qualification to the historical characterisation of Wales as a major electricity exporter.

Analysis published by the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit in April 2026 identifies a substantial decline in Welsh net electricity exports since 2016, associated with the closure of coal and nuclear generating capacity and insufficient replacement generation. Welsh electricity independence

Measurement	Electricity
Peak annual net exports, 2016	Over 21 TWh
Gross Welsh generation, 2024	22.924 TWh
Generation after own use and storage, 2024	20.690 TWh
Consumption including allocated losses, 2024	19.030 TWh
Implied overall net export balance, 2024	1.660 TWh

Welsh electricity independence +1

Historical contraction in net exports

2016 — more than 21 TWh2024 — approximately 1.66 TWhIndicative comparison: a reduction of more than 92% from the historical peak.

This materially changes the assessment.

Wales retains significant generating infrastructure, but the scale of its current annual electricity surplus should not be inferred from historical levels of production.

2. Net exports to England versus exports to Ireland

The distinction between the two destinations matters immensely.

The ECIU assessment indicates that Wales became a net importer from England in 2024, despite remaining an overall net exporter when international interconnector flows were included.

The DESNZ 2024 electricity balance indicates a net transfer of approximately 1.022 TWh from England into Wales. Welsh electricity independence +1

This means that the following statements are compatible:

* Wales generates more electricity than it consumes annually.
* Wales exports electricity internationally.
* Wales receives more electricity from England than it sends to England over a particular year.

The Welsh network serves both as a generation region and as an international electricity transit region.

3. International interconnection: a substantial Welsh infrastructure asset

Wales now hosts two operational electricity interconnectors between Great Britain and the Republic of Ireland.

Interconnector	Operational since	Nominal capacity
East West Interconnector	2012	500 MW
Greenlink	2025	500 MW
Combined		1,000 MW

Gov.ie +2

Both links are bidirectional. Schematic representation, not a geographical route map.

Greenlink’s entry into commercial operation in January 2025 doubled nominal interconnection capacity between Wales and Ireland.

The latest Digest of UK Energy Statistics, published in 2026, records 4.5 TWh of net electricity exports through the Wales–Ireland connection in 2025. GOV.UK Assets

That is equivalent to an average net transfer of approximately 514 MW over the year.

However, electricity exported through a Welsh interconnector is not necessarily electricity generated in Wales. Some may originate elsewhere in the Great Britain network.

This creates a separate strategic asset category: international electricity-market access.

4. Pumped storage: a disproportionate contribution to grid flexibility

Wales hosts two of Britain’s four established large-scale pumped-storage hydroelectric facilities.

Facility	Nominal generating capacity
Dinorwig	1,728 MW
Ffestiniog	360 MW
Combined	2,088 MW

The Welsh Government’s Energy Generation in Wales 2023 report identifies approximately 11 GWh of combined energy storage and describes these facilities as representing around three-quarters of UK pumped-hydro power capacity. GOV.WALES

Combined generating power

2.1 GW

Combined energy storage

~11 GWh

The distinction between power and energy matters: GW measures the rate at which electricity can be delivered, while GWh measures the amount stored.

Pumped storage consumes electricity when pumping water uphill and subsequently returns electricity when water is released through turbines.

Its annual net energy contribution is therefore negative because of conversion losses. Nevertheless, its contribution to grid reliability can be substantial.

Schematic pumped-storage cycle.

The economic function is not to create additional primary energy, but to make previously generated electricity available when it is more valuable to the system.

5. Actual use of Welsh storage infrastructure

Metered Elexon data compiled by GB Electricity indicates the following recent performance at Dinorwig.

Measurement	Twelve months to 16 November 2026
Electricity generated	1.04 TWh
Electricity consumed pumping	1.43 TWh
Net electricity consumption	0.39 TWh
Energy returned relative to pumping	Approximately 73%
Days involving both pumping and generation	363

GB Electricity

This is a particularly useful illustration of why annual net energy accounting cannot adequately measure strategic capability.

Dinorwig consumes more electricity than it generates over the year, yet remains a frequently used component of the national electricity system.

Its contribution is primarily the timing, controllability and availability of electricity, rather than net annual energy production.

These figures come from a secondary compilation of Elexon metering data and have not been independently reconstructed from the underlying half-hourly records.

6. Other Welsh contributions to electricity-system stability

The wider electricity network requires more than sufficient annual generation.

System requirement	Contribution Welsh infrastructure can provide
Peak-demand coverage	Dispatchable gas generation and pumped storage
Frequency response	Rapid adjustment of electricity output or consumption
Operating reserves	Capacity available to respond to unexpected supply shortfalls
Energy balancing	Storage and controllable generation
Renewable integration	Absorption and later return of surplus electricity
Voltage regulation	Suitable generating and converter equipment
International supply flexibility	Bidirectional interconnection with Ireland
System restoration	Appropriately equipped and contracted restoration resources

EirGrid’s transmission assessment confirms that the East West Interconnector supports voltage control, emergency power control and black-start capability. Greenlink also incorporates independently controllable voltage and reactive power functions. cms.eirgrid.ie

The specific volume of each service contracted from Welsh facilities by the National Energy System Operator (NESO) has not been quantified in this check.

Technical capability should not automatically be equated with a current contracted obligation.

7. What annual electricity exports fail to capture

Consider two illustrative generating assets with identical annual output.

Measurement	Asset A	Asset B
Annual electricity supplied	1 TWh	1 TWh
When electricity is available	During favourable weather	On demand, subject to operational limits
Dispatchability	Limited	High
Contribution during demand peaks	Variable	Potentially substantial
Annual energy accounting	Identical	Identical
System value	Potentially different	Potentially different

Neither technology is inherently more valuable in every circumstance. They perform different functions within a combined system.

This establishes the need for separate valuations of energy production and dependable capacity.

For Wales, it also means that declining annual net exports do not necessarily imply an equivalent decline in the strategic value of its electricity infrastructure.

8. Economic valuation of wider grid support

There are established commercial mechanisms through which electricity-system services can be remunerated.

Value stream	Measurement
Wholesale electricity	MWh delivered and associated market prices
Capacity Market	Contracted dependable capacity
Balancing Mechanism	Accepted adjustments to generation or consumption
Frequency response	Contracted response capability and delivery
Reserve services	Available reserve capacity
Restoration services	Contracted restoration capability
Interconnection	Revenue associated with cross-market electricity trading
Avoided infrastructure expenditure	Modelled cost of alternative system provision

For the Welsh inventory, a particularly useful further exercise would be to identify the revenue obtained by Welsh-located assets from these mechanisms.

However, actual commercial revenue and wider system benefit are not necessarily identical. An infrastructure asset could provide substantial security-of-supply benefits without its operator capturing the entire economic value of those benefits.

Conversely, commercial payments should not automatically be added to avoided outage costs or replacement valuations, as these may reflect overlapping benefits.

9. Implications for the sovereignty assessment

The evidence supports an assessment of mutual electricity-system dependency rather than a simple unilateral supply relationship.

Wales benefits from access to:

* Generation elsewhere in Britain.
* Shared balancing and reserve resources.
* A larger wholesale electricity market.
* International electricity connections.

The wider British system benefits from Welsh-located generation, pumped storage, transmission infrastructure and international interconnection.

Under a hypothetical independence settlement, these functions could continue within an integrated electricity market, subject to appropriate legal, regulatory and commercial agreements.

Territorial sovereignty, electricity-market participation and operational integration are separate questions.

Ireland’s existing interconnection with Britain demonstrates that international borders do not inherently prevent substantial electricity-system integration.

10. Corrected wording for the master document

The extent to which Welsh electricity is exported or supports the wider grid: Wales has historically been a significant net electricity exporter, although annual net exports have declined substantially from their peak of more than 21 TWh in 2016. DESNZ’s 2024 electricity balance indicates an overall net export surplus of approximately 1.66 TWh. However, Wales was a net importer from England during that year, demonstrating the importance of distinguishing domestic British transfers from international electricity exports.Wales hosts two operational electricity interconnectors with the Republic of Ireland, the East West Interconnector and Greenlink, providing combined nominal bidirectional capacity of 1 GW. “Fiscal — the £22.8 billion Welsh fiscal deficit

The first distinction is particularly important for this section: the estimated Welsh fiscal deficit is not the Welsh Government’s budget deficit.

It is an estimate of the difference between total public-sector expenditure attributed to Wales and total public-sector revenue attributed to Wales under the current UK constitutional and fiscal arrangements.

That includes expenditure and taxation administered by the UK Government, not simply the devolved institutions.

It is a legitimate and important economic measurement, but it is not automatically a forecast of the fiscal position of an independent Wales.

1. The £22.8 billion figure is confirmed

The Welsh Government’s Wales Economic and Fiscal Report 2026, published this month, explicitly confirms the figure using the latest ONS regional public-sector finance statistics, released on 26 May 2026.

Welsh fiscal deficit, 2024–25

£22.8bn

£7,149

£20,168

£13,019

Source: Wales Economic and Fiscal Report 2026, p. 93. Revenue per person calculated from expenditure and deficit figures. GOV.WALES +1

The estimated deficit increased from £20.9 billion in 2023–24 to £22.8 billion in 2024–25.

2. The overall fiscal balance

Using the published per-person figures and the headline deficit, we can reconstruct the approximate aggregate fiscal position.

The remaining 35.4% constitutes the estimated fiscal shortfall.

The 2022–23 figure comes from an earlier Wales Office analysis. It should be reconciled against the revised ONS historical series before undertaking precise longitudinal analysis.

The increase between the two latest financial years was approximately £1.9 billion, or 9.1%, in nominal terms.

4. What is included in the £22.8 billion?

The ONS statistic covers the public sector as a whole, not merely devolved government.

Included category	Examples
Devolved expenditure	Health, education and Welsh Government programmes
Local government	Council services and local infrastructure
Reserved expenditure	Defence, central government functions
Social security	State pensions and welfare payments
Debt servicing	Attributed UK public debt interest
Capital expenditure	Public infrastructure and investment
Public-sector revenue	Income tax, VAT, corporation tax, National Insurance and other receipts

The ONS includes expenditure attributed to beneficiaries within a country or region, alongside directly identifiable expenditure. Some expenditure is incurred outside the territory concerned. Office for National Statistics

This is therefore not simply a record of money physically spent within Wales.

5. Actual expenditure versus attributed expenditure

This distinction will be particularly important when examining the components of the deficit.

The Welsh Government’s latest fiscal report explicitly confirms that defence expenditure and debt interest are attributed on a population basis.

Consider a simplified example:

Illustrative allocation — not actual defence expenditure

Total UK programme

£50bn

Welsh population share

4.7%

Expenditure attributed to Wales

£2.35bn

That £2.35 billion would be attributed to Wales regardless of whether the associated expenditure physically occurred within Welsh territory.

This is a recognised statistical allocation method. It is not, by itself, evidence of an accounting error.

However, it answers a different question from how much money is spent geographically within Wales or how much a future Welsh state would spend on equivalent functions.

6. Wales compared with the wider UK

The latest Welsh Government report establishes the following:

Indicator, 2024–25	Wales	UK
Public expenditure per person	£20,168	£18,628
Difference	+£1,540	—
Relative expenditure	Approximately 108%	100%
Welsh deficit per person	£7,149	—

GOV.WALES

Wales had the fourth-highest public expenditure per person, behind Scotland, London and Northern Ireland.

It also had the second-highest fiscal deficit per person, behind Northern Ireland.

Only London and the South East recorded fiscal surpluses in 2024–25 under this accounting framework.

This establishes that regional fiscal deficits are widespread within the current UK fiscal structure, although the magnitude of Wales’s deficit is substantial.

7. What the fiscal deficit does not establish

This is where the preceding resource inventory becomes relevant.

Question	Answered by the £22.8bn figure?
Does attributed public expenditure exceed revenue?	Yes
How much does the Welsh Government itself borrow?	No
What is Wales’s international trade balance?	No
What is the value of Wales’s natural resources?	No
What would replacing Welsh strategic infrastructure cost?	No
What benefits does the rest of Britain receive from Welsh infrastructure?	Not comprehensively
What would an independent Wales spend on defence?	No
What share of UK public debt would Wales inherit?	No
What would an independent Wales’s fiscal deficit be?	No

The ONS explicitly excludes regional debt and borrowing estimates from this statistical series. Office for National Statistics

The £22.8 billion therefore cannot be described as either the Welsh national debt or the amount borrowed by the Welsh Government.

Nor does it measure the total economic value of Wales to the United Kingdom.

8. Relationship with the strategic-resource inventory

We have been establishing several different forms of economic value throughout the preceding checks.

Resource or capability	Relevant accounting framework
LNG and petroleum infrastructure	Industrial output, GVA, taxation and infrastructure value
Electricity storage	Capacity, balancing and commercial revenues
Water resources	Abstraction, supply contracts and resilience
Woodland	Commercial production and natural-capital accounts
Flood regulation	Ecosystem-service and replacement-cost valuations
Agricultural production	Output, GVA and food-system resilience
Military training infrastructure	Public expenditure, operational capability and replacement costs

Some of the economic activity associated with these resources is already reflected in attributed tax receipts. Other benefits, particularly non-market ecosystem services and infrastructure availability, are not fully represented in the fiscal account.

That does not mean their monetary valuations can be deducted from the £22.8 billion deficit.

For example, the previously identified £33.54 billion woodland natural-capital valuation represents an asset stock. The fiscal deficit represents an annual flow. Subtracting one from the other would be economically invalid.

The appropriate approach is to maintain complementary fiscal, commercial, natural-capital and strategic-capability accounts.

9. Relevance to an independent Wales

The existing deficit is a necessary starting point for fiscal modelling, but not a complete independence scenario.

Such a scenario would require separately modelling:

Fiscal component	Required assessment
Existing taxation	Revenue retained and changes to the tax base
Reserved expenditure	Cost of providing equivalent sovereign functions
Defence	Future defence policy and commitments
Debt interest	Negotiated debt and asset settlement
Pensions	Future liabilities and transitional arrangements
Public administration	Establishment and operation of sovereign institutions
Natural-resource revenue	Ownership, taxation and regulatory arrangements
Trade	Changes to market access and economic activity
Transition costs	One-off institutional and economic expenditure
Borrowing	Financing requirements and borrowing costs

Some changes could reduce the estimated expenditure or increase revenue. Others could increase expenditure or reduce revenue.

The direction and magnitude of the overall change cannot be established without a detailed model.

The £22.8 billion deficit should therefore neither be dismissed nor treated as an immutable feature of Welsh economic geography.

The £22.8 billion Welsh fiscal deficit: The Welsh Government’s Wales Economic and Fiscal Report 2026, using ONS country and regional public-sector finance statistics released in May 2026, confirms an estimated Welsh net fiscal deficit of £22.8 billion for the 2024–25 financial year, up from £20.9 billion in 2023–24.Public-sector expenditure attributed to Wales amounted to £20,168 per person, with a fiscal deficit of £7,149 per person. These figures imply public-sector revenue of approximately £13,019 per person. Rounded aggregate estimates indicate approximately £64.3 billion of expenditure and £41.5 billion of revenue.The fiscal balance incorporates devolved, local and reserved public-sector activity, including expenditure attributed to Wales through statistical allocation methods. Defence expenditure and public debt interest are among the items allocated on a population basis.The estimated fiscal deficit is not the Welsh Government’s budget deficit, actual Welsh Government borrowing, a measure of national debt or a comprehensive valuation of Wales’s economic contribution to the United Kingdom.It provides an essential baseline for assessing Welsh public finances under current constitutional arrangements. An assessment of the fiscal position of an independent Wales would additionally require modelling taxation, expenditure, sovereign institutional costs, debt and asset succession, trade, natural-resource revenues and transitional arrangements.Natural-capital asset values, commercial infrastructure valuations and non-market strategic benefits should be documented in complementary accounts rather than directly offset against the annual fiscal deficit.

4. How revenue is geographically attributed

This is the particularly important methodological issue for the wider resource inventory.

The £41.487 billion is not produced simply by adding up payments made into government accounts by businesses with Welsh addresses.

The ONS uses administrative data and statistical apportionment methods to distribute UK-wide receipts geographically. The approach differs according to the tax or revenue stream.

Possible attribution basis	What it measures
Taxpayer residence	Where the individual lives
Household consumption	Where relevant expenditure occurs
Business economic activity	Where relevant activity is estimated to occur
Administrative records	Directly identifiable regional receipts
Statistical apportionment	Estimated national or regional share
Geographical resource location	Relevant territorial resource revenues

The ONS methodology explicitly acknowledges that data availability, timeliness and assumptions about who bears taxation affect these calculations. Where newer regional data are unavailable, previous proportions may be carried forward. Office for National Statistics

This is a legitimate statistical methodology, but it is not the same as a complete territorial revenue audit.

5. VAT provides a particularly useful example

The ONS generally allocates indirect taxation on the assumption that consumers ultimately bear the tax.

Consider an illustrative case:

Production in Wales

Goods manufactured

Consumption in England

Goods purchased

The associated consumption taxation would generally be attributed according to consumption rather than the location of manufacturing.

This does not mean the VAT is incorrectly allocated. VAT is a consumption tax, not a direct measure of manufacturing output.

It does, however, demonstrate why the geography of public revenue differs from the geography of productive economic activity.

The ONS also explicitly distinguishes its current regional VAT methodology from the Scottish VAT assignment model, which estimates receipts under a separate VAT jurisdiction. Office for National Statistics

That distinction is directly relevant to modelling a hypothetical independent Welsh tax jurisdiction.

6. Revenue attribution and corporate headquarters

A further question concerns businesses that operate substantial infrastructure in Wales but have their corporate headquarters elsewhere.

Examples from the preceding inventory include petroleum refining, LNG terminals, electricity generation and water infrastructure.

For these businesses, several geographical relationships may coexist:

Measurement	Potential geographical basis
Industrial production	Location of the facility
Employment income	Employees’ residence
Corporation tax	Relevant apportionment methodology
VAT	Consumption
Dividends	Shareholders and ownership
Business rates	Location of taxable property
Resource rents	Ownership and contractual rights

A company having its registered office outside Wales does not automatically establish that every tax receipt associated with its Welsh operations is attributed elsewhere.

Equally, a major industrial facility being located in Wales does not establish that all associated corporate profits and taxes are attributed to Wales.

We would need to examine the ONS methodology for each individual tax.

7. Statistical revisions have materially affected Welsh estimates before

There is a documented example worth retaining in the inventory.

On 18 July 2024, the ONS corrected a processing error involving the geographical allocation of visa fees and Immigration Health Surcharge revenue.

The error predominantly affected Wales and Northern Ireland and had appeared in three successive regional public-finance publications. Revenue, expenditure and fiscal-balance tables were affected. Office for National Statistics

This does not establish that the latest £41.487 billion figure is incorrect.

It does establish that:

* Regional attribution methods require scrutiny.
* Errors can persist across successive publications.
* Historical figures must be checked against revised datasets.
* Statistical uncertainty should be distinguished from demonstrated accounting errors.

The May 2026 release also introduced revised classifications and additional revenue items, including the Bank of England Levy and Gambling Levy. Office for National Statistics

8. What the £41.487 billion does not measure

Economic measurement	Captured by headline public revenue?
Taxation attributable to Wales	Yes
Certain non-tax government receipts	Yes
Total Welsh economic production	No
Gross value of Welsh exports	No
Private-sector corporate profits	Not directly
Total wealth generated within Welsh territory	No
Natural-capital asset values	No
Replacement value of strategic infrastructure	No
Potential future resource royalties	No
Revenue under a different sovereign tax system	No

This distinction connects directly with the preceding work on Welsh natural resources and infrastructure.

The fiscal account measures public receipts arising under existing institutional, economic and taxation arrangements. It does not attempt to value every economic benefit generated by Welsh territory.

However, some of those benefits already generate economic activity and associated taxation included within the £41.487 billion. They must not be counted twice.

9. Implications for a future Welsh fiscal model

The appropriate starting point would be the existing £41.487 billion revenue estimate, followed by a tax-by-tax reconciliation.

Potential adjustment	Required analysis
Tax attribution	Existing methodology compared with territorial tax arrangements
Tax policy	Potential changes in rates, allowances and tax bases
Corporation tax	Treatment of cross-border businesses and profits
VAT	Separate jurisdiction and place-of-supply rules
Crown Estate income	Ownership, management rights and future receipts
Natural-resource taxation	Legally and commercially achievable revenue
International trade	Changes in economic activity and market access
Public assets	Income rights under any succession settlement
Administrative costs	Revenue collection and compliance expenditure
Behavioural responses	Investment, migration, consumption and business decisions

The resulting fiscal position could be better or worse than the existing estimate, depending on the arrangements adopted and their economic consequences.

There is not yet sufficient evidence to quantify that difference.

“Welsh GDP and GVA

For the fiscal assessment, we need both figures, but they perform slightly different functions.

* Gross domestic product (GDP): the value of economic production within Wales at market prices. This is the appropriate denominator for expressing the fiscal deficit as a percentage of the economy.
* Gross value added (GVA): the value generated by economic activity after deducting intermediate consumption. This is particularly useful for assessing individual industries and their contribution to Welsh economic output.

The relationship is:

GDP = GVA + \text{product taxes} - \text{product subsidies}

Neither figure represents government revenue, national wealth or the total value of Welsh natural and strategic assets.

1. Latest verified annual figures

The latest ONS annual regional accounts were published on 23 September 2026, with supplementary GVA data released on 13 November 2026. The Welsh Government updated its corresponding statistical release on 20 November.

+0.5%

Composition of GDP at market prices — 2024

GVA at basic prices

£87.4bn

Product taxes less product subsidies

~£12.9bn

This difference is not equivalent to the total amount of taxation raised in Wales.

Income tax, corporation tax and National Insurance, for example, are not simply added to GVA to calculate GDP.

The adjustment concerns taxes and subsidies on products.

6. Why GVA matters for the resource inventory

GVA helps distinguish the value of industrial production from the gross value of goods moving through Wales.

For instance, consider an illustrative refinery:

Economic activity	Illustrative value
Petroleum products sold	£5bn
Imported crude and other intermediate inputs	£4bn
Gross value added	£1bn

The refinery contributes £1 billion in GVA, rather than £5 billion.

That GVA encompasses employee compensation, gross operating surplus and relevant production taxes less subsidies. It is not equivalent to either company profit or public revenue.

This is particularly relevant to the sectors we have already examined.

Sector	Measurement to prioritise
Petroleum refining	GVA rather than gross fuel sales
LNG terminals	Domestic value added rather than imported gas value
Agriculture	Farm GVA rather than gross agricultural output
Forestry	Commercial GVA alongside separate ecosystem accounts
Electricity	Generation and network-service GVA
Water	Supply-sector GVA alongside resource and resilience accounts
Manufacturing	GVA rather than total exports or turnover
Defence infrastructure	Government production and economic activity alongside operational capability

7. Geographical production versus retained income

This is another important distinction.

GDP and GVA measure production occurring within an economic territory. They do not necessarily establish how much resulting income remains within that territory.

For example, a foreign-owned electricity generating station located in Wales can contribute to Welsh GVA even when some of its profits are subsequently distributed to shareholders outside Wales.

The same applies to a British company headquartered in England with productive facilities in Wales.

For a fuller assessment, we should eventually distinguish:

Measure	What it establishes
GDP	Territorial economic production
GVA	Value added by industries
GNI	Income accruing to resident economic units
GDHI	Disposable household income
Public revenue	Government receipts
National wealth	Accumulated economic assets and liabilities
Natural capital	Environmental assets and associated services

Gross national income (GNI) would be particularly relevant to examining income flows into and out of Wales. I have not established a comprehensive current Welsh GNI estimate.

8. What GDP does not fully capture

The preceding strategic-resource work remains relevant even after establishing the £100.3 billion GDP figure.

Conventional GDP does not comprehensively measure:

* The insurance value of spare infrastructure capacity.
* The availability of strategic mineral reserves.
* Non-market ecosystem services.
* The replacement cost of geographically specific military infrastructure.
* The value of avoiding disruption to essential services.
* The accumulated value of cultural and natural assets.

Some associated economic activity is already included in GDP. Other services require supplementary accounting.

The objective is not to inflate Welsh GDP by adding hypothetical valuations, but to establish a broader account of Welsh productive capacity, wealth and strategic importance.

“Welsh export figures

For the fiscal and sovereignty assessment, we need to distinguish four categories:

* International goods exports.
* International services exports.
* Goods and services supplied to the rest of the UK.
* Domestic value added embodied in exports, rather than their gross commercial value.

The third category is particularly important. England is an external market from the perspective of the Welsh regional economy, but sales to England are not currently international exports.

Consequently, headline international export statistics alone cannot establish the full extent of Welsh trade beyond its borders.

7. Welsh external sales and purchases

The same survey allows us to construct an indicative comparison of external sales and purchases.

This might initially suggest a Welsh external trade surplus of approximately £36.6 billion.

We cannot legitimately conclude that from these figures.

The survey does not constitute a comprehensive regional balance of payments. There are substantial differences in coverage, allocation and reporting between sales and purchases.

The Welsh Government itself demonstrates the scale of this problem through a comparison with HMRC data.

9. Geographical attribution and supply-chain limitations

The Welsh Government explicitly acknowledges that its HMRC goods statistics do not capture Welsh-produced components incorporated into finished products elsewhere in Britain and subsequently exported internationally. GOV.WALES

For example:

Wales

Component production

England

Final assembly

Overseas

Finished product sold

Welsh value added may be embodied in the finished export without appearing separately in Welsh international goods export statistics.

The appropriate supplementary measurement would be trade in value added, supported by regional input-output and supply-use tables.

This would help establish both the Welsh value embodied in exports from elsewhere in Britain and the non-Welsh value embodied in exports attributed to Wales.

“The precise ONS regional public-finance methodology

This is one of the most important methodological checks in the fiscal section because it establishes what the £22.8 billion deficit actually measures, how it is constructed and what conclusions can legitimately be drawn from it.

The relevant ONS statistical series is Country and regional public sector finances (CRPSF).

Its purpose is to geographically allocate UK public-sector revenue and expenditure to the four nations and nine English regions, within a consistent national accounting framework.

It is not a set of independently audited national government accounts for each constituent country.

The distinction is between three geographical concepts:

Concept	Meaning
Revenue attribution	Where public revenue is estimated to arise
Expenditure incidence	Where the intended beneficiaries of public expenditure are located
Expenditure location	Where money is physically spent and economic activity occurs

These three geographies do not necessarily coincide.

1. The methodological framework

The regional accounts are derived from the UK-wide Public Sector Finances (PSF) statistics and follow national accounting concepts associated with the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010).

They cover central government, local government and public corporations.

The three principal outputs are:

Aggregate	Definition
Total current revenue	Taxation, social contributions and other public-sector income
Total expenditure	Current and capital expenditure under national accounting rules
Net fiscal balance	Difference between attributed expenditure and revenue

Transactions are generally recorded on an accruals basis, rather than simply when cash changes hands.

The ONS expressly distinguishes the regional fiscal balance from regional borrowing and does not produce corresponding regional debt accounts. Office for National Statistics

2. How the figures are constructed

UK-wide public-sector accounts

National revenue and expenditure totals

Revenue allocation

Administrative data, tax-specific indicators and estimated incidence

Expenditure allocation

Treasury expenditure data, beneficiary location and allocation rules

Regional fiscal estimates

Wales — attributed revenue

£41.487bn

Wales — attributed expenditure

£64.268bn

Estimated deficit

£22.781bn

Methodological schematic using the working 2024–25 figures established in the preceding checks.

For revenue where direct regional records are unavailable, the general calculation is:

R_{W,i}=R_{UK,i}\times s_{W,i}

Where is total UK revenue from a particular source and is Wales’s estimated share based on a relevant indicator.

Each revenue category may have a different indicator. The resulting regional estimates are constrained to the UK totals.

This ensures national accounting consistency, but does not independently establish the accuracy of every geographical allocation.

3. Important methodological update — June 2026

There has been a change to the ONS’s methodological documentation.

Document	Status
Detailed methodology guide, 7 June 2024	Discontinued on 1 June 2026
Quality and Methods Guide (QMG), 26 May 2026	Current methodological guidance
Country and regional public-sector finances, FYE 2025	Current statistical baseline

The older guide runs to 44 pages and contains considerably more detail about individual allocation methods than the newer guide.

Both are relevant to our investigation, but the older document should not be assumed to describe every current tax calculation unchanged. Office for National Statistics +1

Revenue methodology

4. Directly recorded versus apportioned revenue

The current methodology explicitly distinguishes between region-specific receipts and revenues allocated using indicators.

Only a small number of categories, primarily devolved taxes, use known regional revenue amounts directly. Other receipts are geographically apportioned.

This is important because the precision of the published £41.487 billion total does not imply that every constituent transaction has been geographically identified to that degree of precision. Office for National Statistics

5. Tax-specific attribution

The following table summarises the principal geographical approaches. It is not yet a complete replication of the tax allocation workbook.

Revenue category	Principal geographical basis
Personal income tax	Taxpayer residence
National Insurance	Residence-based attribution
Land Transaction Tax	Welsh-specific revenue
Landfill Disposals Tax	Welsh-specific revenue
VAT	Estimated liabilities across consumer and other sectors
Corporation tax	Statistical allocation of corporate activity
Council tax	Regional and local government data
Public-sector rent	Direct records or economic proxies
Public-sector operating surplus	Multiple indicators, depending on institution and activity

The essential point is that different taxes are assigned according to different economic relationships.

It would therefore be inappropriate to apply a single correction factor to the entire £41.487 billion revenue estimate.

6. VAT — detailed methodology

The archived ONS guide divides VAT revenue, excluding refunds, into four sectors.

Sector	Allocation method
Households	Household spending, household numbers and applicable VAT treatment
Organisations supplying VAT-exempt services	GVA in relevant industries
Government	Identifiable government service expenditure
Housing-related investment	Population share

VAT refunds are calculated separately. Office for National Statistics

The model also assumes that the initial division of VAT receipts between those four sectors is consistent across regions.

That assumption creates a legitimate area for sensitivity analysis, particularly where the industrial composition of Wales differs from the UK average.

It does not establish in advance whether Welsh VAT revenue is overestimated or underestimated.

7. The separate-jurisdiction problem

This is a particularly significant finding for our sovereignty assessment.

The current ONS guide, in section 8, distinguishes its methodology from the Scottish VAT assignment model developed by HMRC, HM Treasury and the Scottish Government.

The latter estimates revenue on the basis of a hypothetical separate VAT jurisdiction. The ONS regional model instead allocates revenue under the existing UK system.

The ONS expressly states that these estimates are not comparable on a like-for-like basis. Office for National Statistics

That provides an official methodological precedent for distinguishing:

Model	Question answered
Existing UK regional tax attribution	What share of existing UK revenue is attributable to Wales?
Separate Welsh tax jurisdiction	What revenue would accrue under a separate Welsh taxation system?
Full independence scenario	How would revenue change following institutional, economic and behavioural adjustments?

These are three distinct modelling exercises.

Expenditure methodology

8. Primary expenditure data source

The ONS principally draws on HM Treasury’s Country and Regional Analysis (CRA).

However, the figures are not identical.

Statistical system	Expenditure aggregate
HM Treasury CRA	Total expenditure on services (TES)
ONS public-sector finances	Total managed expenditure (TME)

TES covers approximately 90% of TME nationally. ONS accounting adjustments reconcile the two frameworks. Office for National Statistics

The remaining difference is not equivalent to unaccounted spending. It reflects differences in accounting coverage and treatment.

Nor should the national 90% proportion automatically be assumed to apply specifically to Wales.

9. Three categories of expenditure

Identifiable expenditure

Spending whose beneficiaries can be associated with a particular region, such as local public services and relevant welfare expenditure.

Non-identifiable expenditure

Spending considered to benefit the UK generally, rather than a specific constituent territory.

Expenditure outside the UK

Overseas expenditure for which a regional share may nevertheless be assigned in the fiscal accounts.

Accounting adjustments and reconciliation

Conversion from departmental expenditure measures to national accounting aggregates.

Total expenditure attributed to Wales

£64.268bn

The ONS regional accounts therefore go beyond geographically identifiable Treasury expenditure.

10. Non-identifiable expenditure allocation rules

The following allocation rules are documented in section 35 of the archived detailed ONS guide.

Expenditure function	Allocation indicator
Defence	Population
Public debt interest	Population, with specific pension-related exceptions
International services	Population
Public and common services	Population
Public order and safety	Population
Enterprise and economic development	Population
Science and technology	GVA
Transport	GVA
Environmental protection	GVA
Agriculture, forestry and fisheries	Population
Health	Population
Recreation, culture and religion	Population
Social protection	Population

These rules apply to the relevant non-identifiable component, not necessarily the whole expenditure function. Certain overseas expenditures use different indicators. Office for National Statistics

For example, identifiable transport expenditure is not simply allocated according to GVA. That allocation rule concerns the relevant non-identifiable expenditure.

The distinction matters because it prevents us from treating all Welsh public expenditure as either geographically recorded or population-apportioned.

11. Population versus economic-output allocation

The allocation indicator can materially change the expenditure attributed to Wales.

Using our previously established approximate shares of UK population and GDP, the following calculator illustrates the difference.

Illustrative sensitivity to allocation method

Hypothetical UK-wide expenditure programme

Total programme expenditure

£50bn

Population-based allocation — 4.6%

£2.300bn

GDP-based alternative — 3.48%

£1.740bn

Difference in attributed expenditure

£0.560bn

Illustrative only. GDP is used here as an economic-output proxy, not as a substitute for the ONS’s actual GVA allocation rules.

Neither allocation is inherently correct for every purpose.

A population allocation may be appropriate when estimating the equal per-person benefit of a national service. An economic-output allocation might be appropriate for a function more closely associated with productive activity.

A territorial expenditure approach would answer a different question again.

12. Defence expenditure and the Welsh defence estate

This has direct implications for our earlier assessment of Sennybridge and RAF Valley.

There are at least four separate measurements:

Measurement	Meaning
Defence spending attributed to Wales	Wales’s estimated share of relevant national expenditure
Defence spending physically incurred in Wales	Personnel, procurement, maintenance and construction expenditure
Value of Welsh-located defence assets	Land, buildings, infrastructure and equipment
Strategic value to UK defence	Operational capability and availability

The population-based allocation of non-identifiable defence spending does not measure the latter three.

Neither does the presence of valuable military infrastructure in Wales establish that the corresponding attributed defence expenditure should simply be removed from the fiscal balance.

An independent-state scenario would require estimating future defence requirements and negotiating the treatment of existing assets.

13. Debt interest versus debt ownership

A similarly important distinction applies to public debt.

The ONS attributes relevant UK public debt interest to Wales, principally using population shares.

However, its regional public-finance series excludes regional debt stocks and borrowing figures.

We therefore have an estimate of annual debt-servicing expenditure attributed to Wales, without a corresponding ONS estimate of Welsh sovereign debt.

Those cannot be treated as an established legal debt-and-interest settlement.

Accounting adjustments and statistical quality

14. Not every expenditure or revenue item is a cash payment

The archived guide documents adjustments involving depreciation, VAT refunds, pensions, rail infrastructure and imputed transactions.

Some public-sector operating surplus also represents consumption of fixed capital rather than commercial profit.

For example, depreciation associated with a public asset can appear in both revenue and expenditure accounting, with offsetting effects on the fiscal balance.

This is why a detailed audit would have to examine both sides of the accounts rather than removing individual expenditure items in isolation.

15. Officially acknowledged limitations

The May 2026 guidance identifies three important limitations:

* Publication typically occurs about 14 months after the reference period.
* Missing contemporary data may be estimated from earlier observations or updated using national trends.
* Alternative allocation principles can produce different regional fiscal estimates.

Despite these limitations, the series is designated as accredited official statistics and remains the principal consistent UK-wide regional fiscal dataset. Office for National Statistics +1

Accreditation establishes that the statistics meet recognised professional standards. It does not mean that all underlying allocations are directly observed or uniquely determined.

16. Changes implemented in May 2026

The latest release incorporates several changes that matter for historical reconciliation.

Change	Accounting area
Bank of England levy	Revenue
Gambling levy	Revenue
Pool Reinsurance Nuclear classification	Public-sector classification
Scottish Warm Home Discount classification	Expenditure
Revised Air Passenger Duty calculations	Revenue
Updated Warm Home Discount data	Expenditure
Revised asset-transfer calculations	Accounting adjustments

These changes demonstrate why we should use a consistent publication vintage when comparing different years. Office for National Statistics

Implications for our wider fiscal assessment

17. Four complementary accounts

I would structure the Welsh assessment into four separate accounting exercises.

Account A — Existing regional fiscal balance

The ONS baseline, including the £22.781 billion attributed fiscal deficit under current arrangements.

Account B — Territorial economic activity

Actual public expenditure geographically incurred, employment, production, procurement and territorial revenue indicators.

Account C — Sovereign fiscal scenario

Revenue under a separate jurisdiction, sovereign institutional expenditure, debt arrangements and transition costs.

Account D — National wealth and strategic capability

Natural capital, infrastructure, resource rights, resilience, cultural assets and operational capabilities.

This preserves the integrity of the existing fiscal statistics while allowing us to investigate questions they were not designed to answer.

18. What we should request from the ONS

To conduct a genuinely reproducible methodological audit, the following information would be useful:

Required data	Purpose
UK revenue total for every tax line	Establish allocation denominator
Welsh allocation coefficient for each line	Reproduce Welsh estimate
Underlying indicator dataset	Assess geographical attribution
Indicator reference year	Identify lagged inputs
Direct-record versus modelled status	Distinguish observed and estimated amounts
Identifiable expenditure	Establish beneficiary-specific spending
Non-identifiable expenditure	Quantify national allocations
Overseas expenditure	Identify attributed external spending
Accounting adjustments	Reconcile Treasury and ONS totals
Revision history	Track methodological changes
Alternative allocation estimates	Assess sensitivity

An especially useful output would be an item-by-item Welsh fiscal reconciliation table, rather than simply another headline deficit estimate.

The relevant ONS team is sub-uk.psf@ons.gov.uk.

19. Corrected wording for the master document

The ONS regional public-finance methodology: The Office for National Statistics constructs country and regional public-sector finance estimates from UK-wide public-sector accounts using revenue attribution, expenditure allocation and national accounting adjustments. The methodology distinguishes directly identifiable regional revenue from statistically apportioned receipts and allocates expenditure according to estimated beneficiaries, geographical location and other relevant indicators.Revenue allocation varies by revenue category, including taxpayer residence, consumption, economic activity and directly recorded regional receipts. Expenditure incorporates identifiable, non-identifiable and overseas spending, with relevant national expenditures allocated using population, economic output and other indicators.The resulting net fiscal balance represents an estimate of public finances under existing UK arrangements. It is not a territorial cash-flow statement, a measure of devolved government borrowing or an independently established sovereign debt liability.The ONS acknowledges that alternative allocation principles may produce different regional estimates and that unavailable contemporary data may require statistical approximation. Its current Quality and Methods Guide was revised on 26 May 2026, replacing the detailed methodology guide discontinued on 1 June 2026.Assessment of an alternative constitutional settlement requires separate modelling of territorial revenues, sovereign expenditure, income flows, asset and liability arrangements, and economic responses. Such analysis should retain the existing ONS fiscal balance as its baseline rather than replacing it with unverified adjustments.

“Whether the Welsh regional deficit is being interpreted correctly

The £22.8 billion deficit is a legitimate measure of Wales’s estimated fiscal position under existing UK arrangements. It becomes misleading when treated as a comprehensive measure of Welsh economic viability, economic contribution or the inevitable fiscal position of an independent Wales.

There are two equally important errors to avoid:

* Treating the regional fiscal deficit as proof that Wales cannot function as an independent state.
* Treating the methodological limitations of the regional fiscal accounts as proof that the deficit does not really exist.

Neither conclusion follows from the statistics.

The issue is not necessarily the accuracy of the headline figure, but the scope of the conclusions drawn from it.

1. What the ONS actually says

The current ONS Quality and Methods Guide, revised on 26 May 2026, confirms that regional public-finance statistics are constructed using two principal approaches:

* Who pays: the estimated geographical incidence of public revenue.
* Who benefits: the estimated geographical incidence of public expenditure.

The ONS explicitly states that the net fiscal balance is not equivalent to regional borrowing. It also excludes regional debt stocks and financial account data. Office for National Statistics +1

There is an even more explicit qualification in the ONS’s 2019 statistical publication:

They may not be an accurate representation of public finances should fiscal powers be fully devolved among UK countries and regions. Office for National Statistics

That qualification concerns full fiscal devolution, even before considering the additional institutional changes associated with independence.

2. The correct interpretation of the headline numbers

Using our existing working fiscal baseline:

Attributed public expenditure

£64.268bn

Attributed public revenue

£41.487bn

Net fiscal deficit

£22.781bn

Financial year 2024–25. Working figures established in the preceding fiscal checks.

The correct interpretation is that public-sector expenditure attributed to Wales exceeded public-sector revenue attributed to Wales by approximately £22.8 billion.

This is a substantial fiscal imbalance.

It demonstrates that, under current arrangements, Welsh-attributed public receipts do not cover the full cost of public expenditure attributed to Wales.

It does not establish that £22.8 billion in cash was transferred from England into Wales.

3. Fiscal redistribution versus an actual financial transfer

These concepts are frequently conflated.

Measurement	Meaning
Regional fiscal deficit	Difference between attributed expenditure and revenue
Welsh block grant	Funding transferred to the devolved administration
Territorial cash flow	Money physically entering or leaving Wales
UK public borrowing	Borrowing undertaken by the UK public sector
Sovereign borrowing requirement	Financing needed by an independent government

The estimated Welsh fiscal deficit reflects the operation of a pooled UK fiscal system, including national borrowing.

It cannot be attributed exclusively to financial transfers from English taxpayers.

Some expenditure attributed to Wales is incurred outside Wales. Some is financed through UK borrowing. Some relates to services provided collectively across the UK.

The deficit nevertheless represents a genuine fiscal benefit of participation in a system that pools expenditure and revenue.

4. The most common interpretations assessed

Interpretation	Assessment
Attributed Welsh expenditure exceeds attributed revenue by £22.8bn	Correct
Wales receives substantial net fiscal support under current arrangements	Supported
Westminster transfers £22.8bn directly to the Welsh Government	Incorrect
Wales borrows £22.8bn annually	Incorrect
Wales owes England £22.8bn annually	Incorrect
Wales consumes £22.8bn more than it produces	Incorrect
The deficit measures Wales’s international trade balance	Incorrect
Wales could eliminate the deficit merely through independence	Unsupported
An independent Wales would necessarily have the same deficit	Unsupported
Wales has no economic value beyond its public revenue	Incorrect
Independence would require serious fiscal adjustment or financing arrangements	Supported as a conditional assessment

The central error is treating a regional public-sector account as though it were an entire national economic account.

5. Fiscal viability versus economic viability

Using our previously established GDP estimate, the public-finance figures produce the following indicative ratios.

Welsh GDP

£100.3bn

Regional deficit relative to GDP

22.7%

Public revenue relative to GDP

41.4%

Public expenditure relative to GDP

64.1%

Indicative calculations combining calendar-year 2024 GDP with financial-year 2024–25 public finances. Not precisely period-matched.

If a deficit of approximately 22.7% of GDP persisted under a separate sovereign fiscal system, it would present an exceptionally serious financing challenge.

That should not be understated.

However, the viability of a sovereign economy depends on more than its initial fiscal balance. Relevant factors include its productive capacity, taxation potential, monetary arrangements, access to financing, external trade, debt settlement, institutional capacity and economic growth.

The deficit establishes the scale of the starting fiscal challenge. It does not settle all those other questions.

6. The geographical expenditure problem

This connects directly with our investigation of Welsh defence infrastructure.

Consider Sennybridge and RAF Valley.

Measurement	Relevant question
Defence expenditure attributed to Wales	What share of UK defence expenditure is assigned to Wales?
Territorial defence expenditure	How much defence spending physically takes place in Wales?
Welsh economic benefit	How much employment, procurement and income does Wales receive?
British operational benefit	What military capability does the wider UK obtain?
Replacement expenditure	What would equivalent capability elsewhere cost?
Future sovereign expenditure	What defence arrangements would an independent Wales require?

The regional public-finance methodology primarily addresses the first question.

It cannot be used to answer all six.

However, the operational value of Sennybridge or RAF Valley cannot simply be deducted from the existing fiscal deficit either. Establishing future lease payments, compensation, shared defence arrangements or other commercial terms would require a separate assessment.

7. Does the fiscal deficit capture the wider value of Wales to Britain?

Not comprehensively.

This is where our preceding resource inventory becomes particularly useful.

Welsh resource or capability	Value not necessarily captured by regional fiscal balance
Water infrastructure	Supply security and drought resilience
Military training estates	Operational capability and substitution constraints
LNG terminals	Availability of import capacity
Petroleum refining	Security of domestic fuel-processing capability
Pumped hydro	Electricity-system flexibility
International interconnectors	Access to neighbouring electricity markets
Anthracite	Domestic industrial mineral availability
Agricultural land	Food-system resilience and productive potential
Woodland	Carbon storage and ecosystem services
Cultural assets	Non-market and accumulated cultural value

Some associated economic benefits are already reflected in taxation, GDP or commercial income.

Others are not fully monetised or are measured through separate accounting frameworks.

Our assessment should therefore recognise these additional forms of value without assuming that they constitute readily available government revenue.

An asset can be strategically indispensable without generating enough taxable income to finance public services. Conversely, a profitable industry can generate substantial public revenue without being strategically indispensable.

8. The stock-versus-flow problem

This is important when comparing the fiscal deficit with the natural-capital and infrastructure valuations we have assembled.

Annual fiscal flow

£22.8bn

Fiscal deficit during one financial year.

Natural-capital asset stock

£33.5bn

Previously identified Welsh woodland valuation, representing discounted future services.

It would be incorrect to subtract the woodland valuation from the fiscal deficit and claim that Wales consequently has a surplus.

It would be equally incorrect to argue that the woodland is economically worthless because its full asset value does not appear in annual public revenue.

Both measurements are useful, but they belong to different accounts.

9. What would happen to the deficit under alternative arrangements?

The correct modelling approach is to begin with the existing deficit and calculate evidenced changes.

D_{\text{future}}=D_{\text{baseline}}+\Delta E-\Delta R

Where:

* represents the fiscal deficit.
* represents changes in public expenditure.
* represents changes in public revenue.

Illustrative fiscal sensitivity model

Starting regional deficit: £22.781bn

Additional annual public revenue

£0.0bn

Annual expenditure reductions

£0.0bn

Additional annual expenditure

£0.0bn

Resulting illustrative deficit

£22.78bn

22.7% of baseline GDP, holding GDP constant.Reset to existing baselineThis is arithmetic sensitivity analysis, not a forecast. None of the adjustable amounts represents an established achievable policy outcome.

This demonstrates the magnitude of changes required without making unsupported assumptions about their feasibility.

10. Testing proposed adjustments

Any proposed adjustment to the existing fiscal deficit should pass several tests.

Proposed adjustment	Necessary qualification
Remove allocated UK defence expenditure	Include future Welsh defence and security costs
Remove UK debt interest	Establish debt settlement and future financing costs
Reallocate corporation tax	Demonstrate the alternative tax base and attribution rules
Introduce resource royalties	Establish ownership, legality, rates and commercial viability
Receive Crown Estate revenues	Account for management costs and existing commitments
Increase economic growth	Model the resulting tax revenue, not gross GDP alone
Receive EU funding	Account for eligibility, contributions and timing
Monetise infrastructure assets	Distinguish one-off proceeds from recurring revenue
Reduce administrative duplication	Include the cost of new sovereign institutions

Both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios need to be subjected to the same evidential standards.

11. The question of the remaining UK

The existing deficit also does not establish how much the remaining United Kingdom would save following Welsh independence.

A national expenditure programme does not necessarily become cheaper in direct proportion to the population leaving the jurisdiction.

For example, certain defence, diplomatic and administrative costs may be relatively fixed. Conversely, geographically identifiable expenditure might cease or transfer to Welsh institutions.

There would also be potential consequences involving commercial arrangements, trade, infrastructure access, debt servicing and shared services.

We therefore need to distinguish three fiscal questions.

Existing regional balance

What expenditure and revenue are currently attributable to Wales?

Future Welsh sovereign balance

What would the new Welsh state’s expenditure, revenue and financing requirements be?

Remaining UK fiscal impact

How would separation affect the remaining UK’s revenues, expenditure and economic capabilities?

There is no requirement for the answers to those three questions to be numerically identical.

12. Corrected wording for the master document

Interpretation of the Welsh regional fiscal deficit: The estimated Welsh fiscal deficit of approximately £22.8 billion for 2024–25 represents the difference between public-sector expenditure and revenue attributed to Wales under existing UK constitutional, economic and fiscal arrangements.The ONS constructs these estimates using geographical revenue incidence and expenditure-benefit allocation methods. It explicitly distinguishes regional fiscal balances from actual regional borrowing and does not provide corresponding regional debt accounts. Previous ONS publications have also acknowledged that regional fiscal estimates may not accurately represent public finances under full fiscal devolution.The deficit establishes a substantial existing fiscal imbalance and provides an essential baseline for assessing alternative constitutional arrangements. However, it does not measure the amount of money physically transferred into Wales, the Welsh Government’s borrowing, the country’s external trade balance or its comprehensive economic contribution to the United Kingdom.The prospective fiscal position of an independent Wales requires separate modelling of taxation, public expenditure, defence, pensions, debt succession, institutional costs, trade arrangements and wider economic responses. The fiscal consequences for the remaining UK likewise require independent assessment.Welsh natural resources, strategic infrastructure, productive capacity and non-market economic benefits are relevant to those wider assessments but cannot be directly offset against annual fiscal deficits without establishing corresponding recurring public revenues or expenditure reductions.Accordingly, the existing regional deficit should be treated neither as conclusive evidence against Welsh economic viability nor as an accounting artefact that can be disregarded.

“Natural capital and strategic value — the £2.5 billion annual ecosystem-service estimate

The first distinction is between the annual economic value of ecosystem services and the capitalised value of natural assets.

The former estimates the benefits generated during a particular year. The latter estimates the present value of expected future benefits.

The £2.5 billion figure therefore needs checking against its original reference year, geographical coverage, valuation methodology and included ecosystem services before we can incorporate it into the Welsh economic inventory.

It should not be interpreted as £2.5 billion of annual government revenue or additional GDP.

1. The £2.5 billion figure is confirmed — for 2022

The Welsh Government’s Sustainable Farming Scheme: Full Business Case, published in September 2025, provides an explicit breakdown in Table 59.

However, this is a historical estimate rather than a fixed annual value. The ONS’s subsequent 2025 natural capital accounts put the Welsh annual value at approximately £2 billion for 2023.

A further edition was published on 19 November 2026, so we should also establish whether that provides a newer Welsh estimate. Office for National Statistics +1

3. How are these services valued?

The ONS natural capital accounts follow the United Nations’ System of Environmental-Economic Accounting framework, complementing conventional national economic accounts.

Different services require different valuation methods.

Service	Principal valuation approach
Agricultural biomass	Resource rent
Water provisioning	Resource rent
Coal and mineral extraction	Resource rent
Renewable electricity	Resource rent
Timber	Physical production and valuation prices
Greenhouse gas regulation	Physical emissions and removals, carbon valuation
Air pollution regulation	Pollution removal and associated health benefits
Recreation	Attributable expenditure
Recreation-related health	Estimated health benefits of physical activity
Aesthetic services	Contribution of natural surroundings to property values

Office for National Statistics +1

The distinction is particularly significant for the strategic resources we have already investigated.

For example, the £272.2 million water provisioning estimate does not measure the total commercial value of Welsh water supplies, the replacement cost of reservoirs or the economic consequences of a prolonged interruption to supplies in England.

It estimates the economic return attributable to the natural resource itself under the accounting methodology.

4. Why does coal have a negative value?

The negative £171.5 million coal provisioning figure is worth highlighting.

Under the resource-rent methodology, estimated economic returns are calculated after accounting for operating costs and the cost of using produced capital.

A negative resource rent can arise where the industry’s return is insufficient to cover these estimated costs.

The ONS acknowledges that both coal and water provisioning can produce negative annual valuations. Office for National Statistics

This does not necessarily mean:

* The underlying mineral reserves have no strategic utility.
* Every individual mine is commercially unprofitable.
* The physical resource has disappeared.
* Replacing domestic supplies through imports would be costless.

The negative valuation and the strategic availability of specialist Welsh anthracite are separate economic questions.

5. What is excluded from the £2.5 billion?

The ONS explicitly describes its natural capital valuations as incomplete. Flood protection, for example, is not currently included in the main national natural capital aggregate, although it has been valued in separate woodland accounts. Office for National Statistics +1

Resource or service	Coverage
Agricultural biomass	Included
Commercial water provisioning	Included
Carbon sequestration and emissions	Included

Recreation and tourism	Included

Biodiversity	Not comprehensively valued
Pollination	Not separately identified in this aggregate
Soil health and long-term fertility	Not comprehensively valued
Drought resilience and reserve capacity	Not separately quantified
Strategic mineral availability	Not separately quantified
Intrinsic ecological value	Outside the valuation’s scope

This means the £2.5 billion estimate cannot be treated as the comprehensive economic value of Welsh nature.

However, incompleteness does not provide grounds for arbitrarily increasing the figure.

6. Annual valuations fluctuate

Publication	Reference year	Welsh annual ecosystem-service value

Consequently, we cannot conclude that Welsh natural capital productivity declined by approximately £500 million between 2022 and 2023 without extracting a consistent revised time series.

Changes in profitability, commodity prices, valuation assumptions and physical ecosystem condition can all influence these estimates.

These measures cannot simply be added together.

The ecosystem-service valuation includes both market-related and non-market benefits. Some commercial activity associated with agriculture, tourism, water and electricity is already represented within GDP.

Other benefits, such as improved health through recreation and pollution removal, extend beyond conventional measurements of economic production.

A proper environmentally extended economic account would identify and reconcile these overlaps.

8. Who receives the benefit?

This is the particularly important outstanding question for our strategic-value inventory.

The location of a natural asset does not necessarily determine the location of its beneficiaries.

Welsh natural asset	Potential beneficiaries
Reservoir catchments	Welsh and English water consumers
Woodland carbon sequestration	Global population
Flood-regulating habitats	Downstream communities, potentially across national borders
Agricultural land	Domestic and international consumers
Recreational landscapes	Residents and visitors
Renewable energy resources	Participants in the interconnected electricity market
Mineral resources	Domestic and international industrial users

The £2.478 billion aggregate does not establish how much of the associated benefit accrues specifically to Welsh residents, the wider UK or international beneficiaries.

For our purposes, a supplementary beneficiary-incidence account would be particularly valuable, distinguishing:

* Location of the natural asset.
* Ownership and management rights.
* Location of beneficiaries.
* Distribution of financial returns.
* Non-market benefits.
* Dependence and availability of substitutes.

This would complement the ONS public-finance methodology, which we have just examined from the perspective of expenditure incidence.

It is not the market sale price of Welsh land, the value of publicly owned property or the amount of money that a Welsh government could raise against those assets.

Valuation methodology

5. How is natural-capital asset value calculated?

The underlying approach is a net present value calculation.

V=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{S_t}{(1+r_t)^t}

Where:

* is the estimated natural-capital asset value.
* is the expected ecosystem-service value in a future year.
* is the applicable discount rate.
* is the assumed remaining asset life.

The valuation consequently depends upon anticipated future benefits, asset longevity, environmental condition, economic assumptions and discounting.

It is not simply the latest annual ecosystem-service estimate multiplied by a fixed number of years.

6. Sensitivity to discounting

The following demonstrates how the valuation of the same annual service flow can change under different assumptions.

Illustrative natural-capital valuation

Constant annual ecosystem-service value

£2.50bn

Discount rate

3.5%

Asset lifetime

100 years

Illustrative present value

£69.14bn

Assumes constant annual benefits and a constant discount rate. This demonstrates valuation sensitivity; it does not reproduce the ONS’s service-specific methodology.

A material change in estimated asset value does not necessarily imply an equivalent physical change in natural resources.

Economic prices, forecast service flows and methodological changes can also alter the result.

7. Why the newer valuation requires scrutiny

The ONS corrected an error on 19 May 2026 affecting the allocation of water provisioning values between UK countries.

The UK-wide result was unaffected, but country-level monetary estimates were affected.

A further notice on 6 August 2026 identified an input-data error relating to recreational and tourism expenditure.

The ONS indicated that the next natural capital accounts would incorporate corrected data and methodological changes. Office for National Statistics +1

This is particularly relevant given that water provisioning and recreation constitute substantial components of the Welsh valuation.

The numerical difference between the two headline estimates is:

Measurement	Amount

This is a difference between published estimates, not a verified 11.3% decline in Welsh natural wealth.

9. Relationship with the woodland valuation

We previously identified an estimated Welsh woodland natural-capital asset value of approximately £33.54 billion for 2021.

These two valuations must not simply be added together.

Asset account	Value
Welsh natural capital, national aggregate, 2022	£95.748bn
